column1: What is Fred Cohen's 1984 formal definition of a computer virus?
column2: A program that infects other programs by modifying them to include a possibly evolved copy of itself.

column1: What theoretical foundation from von Neumann's 1949 work establishes the mathematical basis for self-replicating code?
column2: A Turing-complete system can contain a program capable of reading its own description and producing an identical copy (cellular automata/self-reproducing machines).

column1: Why can a virus inject code into a 'data' section even though the format declares it non-executable?
column2: Because the CPU makes no distinction between code and data—it simply fetches and executes bytes from memory addresses dictated by the instruction pointer; permission manipulation can make data regions executable.

column1: What is the 'reachability invariant' in virus propagation design?
column2: A virus can only replicate into artifacts whose storage is reachable and whose format it understands well enough to inject executable content without corrupting the host beyond usability.

column1: What is the 'activation invariant' and why does it matter for stealth?
column2: Injected code is worthless until something executes it; the gap between injection and activation is the window of highest detection risk, so viruses target frequently executed artifacts to minimize this window.

column1: What is the 'idempotency invariant' in virus replication, and how is it enforced?
column2: A virus must avoid re-infecting already-infected files (which causes bloat and trivial detection); enforced via an infection marker (magic constant, custom section name, ELF note, reserved header flag) checked before injection.

column1: Why did signature-based detection collapse as a sole defense strategy?
column2: Polymorphic/metamorphic malware generates unique encryption envelopes or code mutations per infection, so no two infected files share identical byte signatures beyond short decryption stubs, and malware volume overwhelmed signature maintenance.

column1: What is the core adversarial paradox of anti-virus engineering?
column2: Any deterministic detection rule, once deployed, becomes observable to attackers and therefore vulnerable to circumvention through engineered polymorphism or metamorphism.

column1: What three properties must a reference monitor satisfy, per the Saltzer and Schroeder principles?
column2: It must provide complete mediation, be tamperproof, and be simple enough to verify (always invoked, non-bypassable, and auditable).

column1: How does a capability-based system invert the attacker/defender asymmetry?
column2: It establishes mathematical invariants (privilege cannot be escalated beyond explicitly granted authorities) that hold regardless of implementation bugs, so security emerges from the enforcement mechanism rather than code correctness.

column1: What distinguishes a virus from a network worm in terms of propagation requirement?
column2: A virus requires a host binary to carry its payload (parasitic infection of executables), whereas a worm self-propagates by exploiting remote vulnerabilities without needing to embed in a host file.

column1: Why is the gap between high-level program logic and low-level memory operations in C/C++ considered the dominant attack surface?
column2: C/C++ permit arbitrary pointer arithmetic with no runtime bounds checking, leaving programmers to manually maintain memory safety invariants the language cannot express or verify, enabling buffer overflows, use-after-free, and type confusion exploits.
